name: Dana Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a family firm in a market town, six of us in an old house on the high street, and the owner is Mr Hale, who's sixty-three. Our clients are farms, the garage, two hairdressers and a few landlords. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, mostly from paper, boxes of invoices that come in at the end of January. I like the farm clients best; they bring eggs at Christmas. What wears me out is the January rush and the fact that I still need Mr Hale to check nearly everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you work, day to day? Paper, software?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paper first, then I type it into the accounts software, and I check it with a calculator, which everyone laughs at. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't want to. Kath, the bookkeeper I have lunch with, tried one for a letter and it got the client's name wrong. That was enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. At lunch with Kath I'd say we can stop hearing about it now. I don't post online much, maybe a comment on a friend's post saying sensible people knew all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI isn't my worry anyway. Mr Hale's sixty-three and he's been talking about retiring. If the boss sells to a bigger firm from the city, I don't know if they'd keep the paper clients or a slow junior like me. And I've got a car loan, a hundred and eighty a month, for two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and try to get quicker, maybe ask Mr Hale for one afternoon a week of training. I'd keep the three months of savings and add to it in the months without a big bill. I'd also ask Mr Hale straight out about his retirement plans, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but with a small worry in the background, like a tap dripping in another room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have you put off asking Mr Hale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the answer's bad I'd rather not know yet. That's silly, I know. My dad says you always want to know the weather before you cut hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the firm was sold, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at the other two firms in town first, and the farm supplies co-op, which has its own accounts office. I wouldn't want to drive to the city every day. That's an hour each way and the car's already costing enough.

say: I'd tell Kath we can finally **stop hearing** about AI.
I'd comment online that **sensible people** knew all along.
think: My real worry is **Mr Hale retiring** and selling to a city firm.
A **car loan** of £180 a month has two years left to run.
do: Ask Mr Hale for **one afternoon a week** of training to get quicker.
Keep the **three months of savings** and add in quiet months.
Ask Mr Hale directly about his **retirement plans**.
feel: **Steady**, with a small worry dripping in the background.
S0.quote: If the boss sells to a bigger firm from the city, I don't know if they'd keep the paper clients or a slow junior like me.
fieldNote: Her worry is **succession**, not AI: a 63-year-old owner who may sell.
She **avoids bad news** but knows it, quoting her father about the weather.
Her limit is **local work**; an hour's drive to the city is a firm no.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hale for an afternoon of training each week
Add to the three months of savings in quiet months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, it depends how it actually works out. At work I'd probably say our clients like paper and a face. I wouldn't go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a city firm with software would do our clients' returns cheaper, and Mr Hale would either sell or cut the slowest person, which is me. The card says checking and writing, and that's my whole day. I'm not sure the farm clients' loyalty lasts past a fee that's half ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what Mr Hale does before I panic. I'd stop the takeaway Fridays and the new boots I've been eyeing, maybe sixty pounds a month, and put it in savings. And I'd ask at the farm supplies co-op whether their accounts office needs someone, because they'd want a local person who knows the farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a lot of the time. I'm not good at not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few months. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hale bought one of those programs and asked me to learn it. That'd tell me he's thinking about doing more with fewer people. Then I'd go straight to the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the program if he asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, because I'd have to. But I'd be slow. I'd still check the new program with my calculator, so it wouldn't save the boss any time with me. That's sort of the problem, isn't it.

say: I'd say **we'll see** how it actually works out.
I'd tell colleagues our clients still want **paper and a face**.
think: A city firm with software could charge **half our fee**.
Mr Hale would sell or cut the **slowest person**, which is me.
do: Wait a few months to see what **Mr Hale does**.
Cut takeaways and the boots, saving about **£60 a month**.
Ask the **farm supplies co-op** about their accounts office.
feel: **Anxious** a lot of the time, because she's bad at not knowing.
S1.quote: I'd still check the new program with my calculator, so it wouldn't save the boss any time with me.
fieldNote: She sees **checking and writing** as her whole day, so the card lands directly on her.
Her trigger to act is the **owner buying software**, which she reads as a sign of cuts.
She sees honestly that her **resistance** cancels the time the tools would save.

steps.text: Wait to see whether Mr Hale buys accounting software
Drop Friday takeaways and the new boots
Save the £60 a month that frees up
Ask the farm supplies co-op about an accounts job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and someone needs to put the brakes on. I don't usually take sides, but two years isn't fair on anyone. At work I'd just be quiet, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job, probably within a year of it arriving. Mr Hale would sell, or retire, and nobody would need a junior who does paper. The co-op's accounts office goes the same way. My mum and dad's sheep farm is hands-on, so it's got a few more years, which is the only bit that isn't screen work in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give up the flat when the lease ends and move back to my parents' farm to save the rent, about five hundred a month. I'd sell the car and use dad's old one. And I'd help on the farm with the paperwork and lambing while I look for anything local, the shop, the vet's front desk, anything with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It'd feel like going backwards ten years, back in my old bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be glad to have me home, she'd never say so. Dad would be practical, he'd have me on the quad bike checking ewes the first morning. I'd be grateful and embarrassed at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the vet's front desk. Isn't that answering customers too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, it probably goes as well. I'm just listing places I know people. I haven't got a real plan for losing the accounts job. I've got a list of doors to knock on.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and someone should put the brakes on.
At work I'd **stay quiet**, as I usually do.
think: I'd **lose my job** within a year of AGI arriving.
My parents' **sheep farm** is the only hands-on work in my life.
do: Give up the flat and **move back home**, saving about £500 a month.
**Sell the car** and use Dad's old one.
Help with **lambing and paperwork** while knocking on local doors.
feel: **Frightened**, like going back ten years to her old bedroom.
S2.quote: I haven't got a real plan for losing the accounts job. I've got a list of doors to knock on.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly and sees no accounting work surviving.
Her safety net is **family**: the parents' sheep farm and their spare room.
When challenged, she admits her list is **not a plan**, which is honest.

steps.text: Move back to the parents' farm when the lease ends
Sell the car and drive Dad's old one
Help with lambing and farm paperwork for her keep
Ask the village shop and vet's about local jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least, and we should use it sensibly. I'd tell people not to panic but not to ignore it. That's me, middle of the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the job around 2031 instead of 2029, so the same thing just later. The good bit is I could finish paying the car and build up savings first. I don't think I'd learn the AI even with five years, I'd just be better prepared to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the car by 2028 and then put that hundred and eighty a month into savings, aiming for nine months. I'd move to the co-op if they'd have me, because it's farmers and they'll want a person longer than a firm does. And I'd wait, honestly, and watch what Mr Hale does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slower kind. Like seeing a storm across the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the co-op want a person longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the farmers there don't trust screens. Half of them still pay by cheque. In five years, I think they'd still want to ring someone they know about their feed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you regret, waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not learning the programs while it was easy to learn. But I know myself. I'd rather be good at the old way of doing accounts than bad at the new way. Maybe that's a mistake.

say: I'd say five years is something, and we should **use it sensibly**.
I'd tell people **not to panic** but not to ignore it either.
think: I'd **lose the job** around 2031 instead of 2029.
I wouldn't **learn the AI**, just be better prepared to leave.
do: Pay off the **car by 2028** and save the £180 a month after.
Move to the **co-op accounts office** if they'll have me.
Watch what **Mr Hale** does before anything bigger.
feel: **Anxious**, like a storm seen across the valley.
S3.quote: I'd rather be good at the old way of doing accounts than bad at the new way. Maybe that's a mistake.
fieldNote: The extra years mainly let her **clear the car loan** and save more.
She bets on **farmers' trust** in a known voice to keep the co-op job going.
She knows her **resistance** might be a mistake and says so plainly.

steps.text: Clear the car loan by 2028, then save the £180
Apply for the co-op accounts office job
Watch Mr Hale's retirement plans before deciding more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and people should get on with their lives. At work I'd say let's do our jobs. Honestly I'd probably tell myself the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels like forever, which is exactly the problem. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd have done nothing about it because there was always time. But my next few years would be fine, probably, and my parents would be nearer retirement than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, get qualified slowly, and keep saving. I'd probably wait, and not plan anything until it gets closer. Maybe around 2033 I'd think about the farm, because hands-on gets until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about now, uneasy about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is the problem. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm a putter-off. With two years I'd have to move. With ten, I'd put it off for nine and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the next ten years that worries you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale selling, still, and whether I ever earn enough to buy a place in town. Houses on Station Road are going for more every year. AI is the far worry, the house is the near one.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to get on with life.
At work I'd say let's just **do our jobs**.
think: Ten years feels like forever, which is **exactly the problem**.
My **next few years** would probably be fine.
do: Keep working and **qualify slowly** while saving.
Wait and plan nothing until AGI **gets closer**.
Think about **the farm** around 2033, since hands-on lasts to 2039.
S4.quote: I'm a putter-off. With two years I'd have to move. With ten, I'd put it off for nine and a half.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **near-term job** feel safe, so her mood eases.
She's clear-eyed about her own **procrastination** as the real risk.
Her near worry is **housing** in town and the firm's sale, not AI.

steps.text: Keep doing tax returns and qualify slowly
Keep saving towards a house in town
Hold off on any big decision until around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With two years I'd have no time to pay things off or find something local. What would help is help for people in small towns to find work near home, not training courses in the city. And some notice from employers, proper notice, before they cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that some of us don't want to change. Not everyone is going to retrain into something exciting. Some of us just want a steady job near our parents.

headlineQuote: Not everyone is going to retrain into something exciting. Some of us just want a steady job near our parents.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old junior** at a six-person family firm in a market town.
She works from **paper and a calculator**, never uses AI, and doesn't want to.
Her nearest worry is the owner **retiring and selling**, more than anything about AI.
In the fast picture she'd **move home** to her parents' sheep farm.
More time makes her **calmer**, but she admits she'd put off acting.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to pay things off or find local work.
whatWouldHelp: Help finding **work near home** in small towns, not city courses.
